Iran. A transcontinental country in western Asia, historically known as Persia, spanning the Iranian Plateau between the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf. One of the world's oldest continuous civilizations, Iran gave rise to the first great multinational empire under the Achaemenid Persians from around five hundred fifty to three hundred thirty BCE and later became the center of Islamic civilization.

Iran's territory encompasses the vast Iranian Plateau, bounded by the Caspian Sea to the north, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman to the south, and mountain ranges—the Alborz and Zagros—that define much of its topography. The Achaemenid Persian Empire from around five hundred fifty to three hundred thirty BCE, founded by Cyrus the Great, was the largest empire the world had yet seen, spanning from Egypt to India until conquered by Alexander the Great.

Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest monotheistic religions, originated in ancient Iran and profoundly influenced later religions including Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. The Silk Road trade routes passed through Iran, making it a crucial hub linking the Mediterranean, East Asia, and India for nearly two millennia. Persian poetry and literature, including the works of Rumi, Omar Khayyam, and Hafiz, rank among humanity's greatest literary achievements and remain widely read today.

The Iranian Islamic Revolution of nineteen seventy-nine established an Islamic theocracy under Ayatollah Khomeini and fundamentally reshaped Middle Eastern politics and Iran's international relations. Iran is home to some of the world's largest proven oil reserves and natural gas deposits, making it a major global energy producer. The Persian language, or Farsi, is one of the world's oldest languages still in continuous use, with a literary tradition spanning over twenty-five hundred years.
